notes.h: Post-Famine agriculture: fewer people, more pasture
notes.b: The Great Famine (1845 to about 1850, caused by potato blight) killed and drove out about a quarter of the population and devastated the cottiers, the poorest tenants who rented tiny plots. Before it, Ireland had depended on the potato, and holdings had been subdivided into ever smaller plots. What was left was a smaller, more commercial farming economy built on livestock.
points: Population fell steadily: about 8.2 million in 1841, about 6.5 million in 1851, about 5.8 million in 1861 and about 5.4 million in 1871. Deaths and emigration in the Famine started the fall, and it did not stop.

Tillage (growing crops) declined and pasture (grass for animals) expanded, because cattle, sheep and dairy produce rose in price relative to grain and needed far less labour. The repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 had already pushed grain prices down relative to livestock prices.
Live cattle were exported to Britain, where the growing towns were the market. The trade was carried by the new railways and steamships, which is why a pasture economy paid so well after the Famine.
Small holdings disappeared as cottiers died or emigrated and landlords joined their plots into larger farms. The number of cottiers and tiny holdings fell sharply, and larger farms became the norm.

Agricultural labourers fell in number because pasture needed fewer hands, yet those who remained were still poor. The small farmers of the west stayed close to subsistence, meaning they grew barely enough to feed their families.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the post-Famine economy in terms of consolidation, pasture and the stronger farmers. Explain why farming changed (relative prices and labour) rather than just saying tillage fell. Do not give a percentage for the loss of small holdings.

notes.h: The stronger farmers and the survival of landlordism
notes.b: Not everyone lost from the Famine. A class of stronger farmers, holding large farms, gained most, while the landlords (a small class who owned almost all the land and let it to tenants) kept their power.
points: The stronger farmers held large farms on long tenure (a secure, long-lasting right to farm the land), so they could profit from rising livestock prices. They were the main gainers of the period.
They dominated parish life and later supplied much of the support for land and nationalist movements, because they had both the wealth and the standing to lead local opinion.

The Encumbered Estates Act (1849), a Famine-era measure, let debt-ridden estates be sold off. The Landed Estates Court (1858) replaced the Encumbered Estates Court and continued the sales, so do not confuse the two.
Some buyers were commercial investors who raised rents and cleared tenants; others were existing landlords or wealthy tenants.

Landlordism survived the Famine: landlords still owned almost all the land, and tenants had no legal security of tenure (no legal right to stay on the farm so long as they paid rent). The Land Act of 1870 gave only limited protection.

Evictions fell from their Famine peak but remained a threat, so tenant right (the tenants' claim to security and to compensation for their improvements) stayed a central grievance of the 1850s and 1860s.
notes.tip: Be ready to define landlordism as used after the Famine: a small landlord class owning almost all the land, with tenants lacking legal security of tenure. Keep the Encumbered Estates Act (1849) and the Landed Estates Court (1858) apart, with their dates.

notes.h: Marriage, the dowry and family life
notes.b: The Famine hardened a pattern of late marriage, celibacy and single-heir inheritance. It kept farms intact, and it pushed other children abroad.
points: A dowry was money or land that a bride's family gave on her marriage. Farmers used it to portion (provide for) a sister, to buy out siblings or to pay debts.
Farms usually passed intact to one son, so a farmer could marry only when his father handed over the holding and a bride with a dowry was found.
Matchmaking was widespread, so families arranged the match, and it depended on land and money more than on affection.
Marriage was late, often in the thirties, and a large share of men and women never married (celibacy), especially in the west. The wait for the farm and the need for a dowry caused this.
Younger sons and daughters without a dowry had to choose between emigration, farm labour, the priesthood or religious life, and domestic service.
Late marriage and celibacy kept the birth rate down, so the population did not recover after the Famine.
notes.tip: Marks go to explaining why the dowry system produced late marriage and celibacy, not just stating it. Link the dowry to single-heir inheritance, then to who could marry, then to the low birth rate.

notes.b: Large-scale emigration continued long after the Famine and became part of normal life. Here the focus is its scale, who left and its effects on those who stayed.
points: About a million people left Ireland in the 1850s, and emigration stayed high through the 1860s.
The United States was the main destination, followed by Britain, Canada and Australia. Liverpool and Cork (Queenstown, now Cobh) were major ports of departure.
Emigrants were mostly young and unmarried, and women left in numbers roughly equal to men. This is why the countryside lost its future workers and parents.
Chain migration meant that relatives and neighbours already abroad sent news and prepaid passages, so each emigrant helped the next to follow.
Remittances (money sent home) helped families pay rent and passage costs for further relatives. Chain migration is the mechanism and remittances are the money.
Emigration relieved pressure on land, but it drained the countryside of young people and fed the idea of exile in nationalist politics (the belief that people had been forced out by British rule).
notes.tip: Stay at the level of scale, who left, chain migration and the effects on those who stayed. Do not drift into the story of the Irish abroad.

notes.h: Primary education: the national school system
notes.b: The national school system, set up in 1831, became the main provider of primary education and a major influence on literacy and language.
points: The system was set up in 1831 through a letter from the Chief Secretary, Edward Stanley, to the Duke of Leinster. It was run by a Board of Commissioners of National Education.
Its aim was combined literary and moral education for children of all denominations, with religious instruction given separately by each church.
The state paid grants, supplied textbooks and inspected schools, and a teacher-training establishment opened in Dublin.
The churches contested the plan. The Church of Ireland set up its own Church Education Society (1839), and Presbyterians objected at first.
The Catholic bishops were divided: Archbishop Daniel Murray of Dublin co-operated, while Archbishop John MacHale of Tuam opposed.

In practice most schools became denominational in character, because local clergy managed them and most pupils in each district were of one faith. After 1850 Cardinal Cullen pressed for greater Catholic control of education.
notes.tip: Questions ask for the system's aims and the churches' reactions. Give the 1831 date and name Stanley and the Commissioners, and say Presbyterians objected 'at first'.

notes.h: The Christian Brothers, literacy and the Irish language
notes.b: Alongside the national schools, other bodies taught the poor, and the language of the classroom had a lasting effect on Irish.
points: The Christian Brothers, founded in Waterford in 1802 by Edmund Rice, ran their own free schools for poor Catholic boys. They stayed outside the national system and spread in the towns.
Do not confuse the two: the national schools were the state-backed primary system of 1831, while the Brothers' schools were a separate Catholic network.
Lessons were in English, so Irish had no place in school. The system reinforced the decline of the Irish language by teaching through English and treating Irish as no help to a career.
School attendance and literacy rose steadily, though no reliable figure for the number of pupils should be given.
notes.tip: For the effects of schooling, give both sides: literacy rose steadily, but teaching through English weakened Irish. Do not quote a pupil or literacy figure.

notes.h: Higher education: the Queen's Colleges and the Catholic University
notes.b: Higher education divided on religious lines. The state founded colleges that were open to all, the Catholic Church objected, and a rival Catholic institution followed.
points: Peel's government founded the Queen's Colleges at Belfast, Cork and Galway by an Act of 1845. They opened in 1849 and formed the Queen's University of Ireland in 1850.
They were non-denominational and had no chapel or chair of theology, so critics called them 'godless colleges'.
The Catholic hierarchy was divided, but Rome condemned the colleges in 1847 and the Synod of Thurles in 1850 forbade Catholics to attend. Cullen backed a Catholic alternative.
The Catholic University opened in Dublin in 1854 with John Henry Newman as first rector. It gave no state-recognised degrees and had few students, and Newman resigned in 1858.
Trinity College Dublin, an Anglican institution, remained the main university for Protestants. Catholics could take degrees but not fellowships.
The Queen's College in Belfast served the Presbyterian middle class of Ulster, which is why it was the most successful of the three.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the two: the Queen's Colleges were state-founded and non-denominational (1845), while the Catholic University was Church-founded (1854). Give the date for each body.

notes.b: The railway network was built from 1834 and its core was largely complete by about 1860. It changed trade, towns and communications.
points: The Dublin and Kingstown Railway opened on 17 December 1834 and ran about six miles from Westland Row in Dublin to Kingstown (now Dún Laoghaire). It was the first railway in Ireland.
Growth began slowly and then became rapid in the late 1840s and 1850s: the network reached about 1,000 miles by the mid-1850s and the main network was complete by about 1860.
The Great Southern and Western reached Cork in 1849 and the Midland Great Western reached Galway in 1851. The Killarney line opened in 1853.
The Dublin to Belfast through route was completed in 1855, so the two cities were joined, crossing the Boyne by the viaduct at Drogheda.
Ireland adopted a gauge (the distance between the rails) of 5 feet 3 inches, fixed in the 1840s, which was different from the British standard gauge.
notes.tip: Name the Dublin and Kingstown Railway (1834) and do not mix it up with the Ulster Railway, which was built later in Belfast. Use 'about 1,000 miles by the mid-1850s' and give no figure for 1845.

notes.h: Railways: effects on the economy, towns and society
notes.b: Railways mattered because they made moving goods and people cheaper and faster. Their effects were uneven, which is the mark of a good answer.
points: Railways cut the cost and time of moving cattle, butter, grain and fish. They tied farmers to British markets through the ports.
Fairs and markets shifted to railway towns, and junction towns such as Mallow, Limerick Junction and Athlone grew in importance.
Some small ports lost trade as goods moved inland by rail instead of by coast.
Newspapers, mail and ideas travelled faster, so national newspapers reached the provinces and political movements could organise nationally.
Tourism grew, for example with the Killarney line opening in 1853. The rail and steamer link to Britain also eased travel and emigration.
notes.tip: Railways are very commonly asked. Give two or more specific effects, each backed by a fact, and show that they were uneven: railway towns grew while small ports lost trade.

notes.b: Dargan was the most successful Irish railway contractor of his day and a public figure who promoted Irish industry. His career rose with the railway boom and ended with the failure of some of his ventures and a fall from his horse in 1866.
points: Born in 1799 near Carlow town, he trained as a surveyor and engineer in England and worked under Thomas Telford on the Holyhead road.

He won the contract for the Dublin and Kingstown Railway, which opened in 1834, and went on to build lines including the Dublin and Drogheda and the Ulster Railway. He became the leading contractor in Ireland and employed thousands of workers.
He also built the Ulster Canal and dredged the Victoria Channel at Belfast in the 1840s. The spoil created Queen's Island, later the Harland and Wolff site.
In 1853 he paid for the Dublin Industrial Exhibition on Leinster Lawn, which drew over a million visitors, and Queen Victoria visited it. Do not confuse it with the Great Exhibition in London (1851).
He lost money on the Exhibition, and his reputation as an Irish industrial pioneer was the main reward. He reportedly refused a baronetcy.
A fall from a horse in 1866 and the failure of some of his ventures ended his career. He died in Dublin on 7 February 1867.

Contemporaries praised him as a self-made Catholic businessman who acted from public spirit. A Dargan testimonial fund helped to fund the National Gallery of Ireland, which opened in 1864, and his statue stands outside it.
Historians see him as a symbol of Irish enterprise, but they note limits: his work rested on railway investment and not on a wider Irish industrial base.
notes.tip: Dargan questions want career dates, projects, the 1853 Exhibition and a judgement. Pair the contemporary view (public-spirited self-made man) with the historians' view (a symbol, but limited by dependence on railway investment).

notes.b: Belfast became an industrial city of linen, engineering and shipbuilding, unlike the largely agricultural south. The key is to link each cause to its result.
points: Mechanised flax spinning arrived in the 1820s and 1830s, and linen became the main industry of Belfast and the Lagan valley.
The American Civil War (1861–65) cut off cotton supplies, a crisis called the cotton famine, so demand and prices for linen rose.
Harbour works, including Dargan's Victoria Channel, allowed larger ships to reach the port, and engineering firms grew up to serve the mills.
Edward Harland took over Robert Hickson's shipyard on Queen's Island in 1858, and in 1861 he and Gustav Wolff formed Harland and Wolff.
Ulster had skilled Protestant labour, capital from the linen trade, local business networks and strong trade links with Britain.
Belfast had no local coal or iron, but cheap imports by sea and rail made industry viable.
Belfast's population grew from about 100,000 in 1851 to over 170,000 by 1871, with migrants coming mainly from the Ulster countryside and Famine-hit areas.
notes.tip: Belfast is a very common question: why did it differ from the rest of Ireland? Name linen, the cotton famine, engineering, shipbuilding, Harland and Wolff and population growth, and link causes to results rather than listing them.

notes.h: Belfast: the south, and sectarian divisions
notes.b: Industry did not spread across the island, and Belfast's growth brought tensions of its own.
points: Industry in the south declined under competition from British factory goods once tariffs were gone. Dublin and Cork kept only brewing, distilling and food processing.
Catholics, mostly migrants from the countryside, made up about a third of Belfast's population. They were concentrated in unskilled jobs and in certain districts such as the Pound.
Sectarian riots broke out in Belfast in 1857 and 1864, tied to Orange marches and to Catholic rivalry for housing and work.
notes.tip: Use the contrast with the south as part of any answer on Belfast: the south faced British competition and kept only brewing, distilling and food processing.

notes.h: Assessment: how far did Ireland recover, 1850–1870
notes.b: Judgements differ on whether post-Famine Ireland was a story of recovery or of continuing weakness. Good answers pair each gain with its limit.
points: Achievement: farm incomes and living standards of the stronger farmers rose, and railways opened national markets.
Limit: the population kept falling, emigration continued and the rural poor of the west gained little.
Achievement: the national school system spread literacy to most of the population.
Limit: schooling in English weakened the Irish language.
Achievement: Belfast industrialised and grew faster than any other Irish town.
Limit: industrialisation was confined to the north-east, and the rest of Ireland depended on agriculture and on exporting people.
Contemporary view: many saw the stronger farmers' prosperity and the railways as evidence of improvement under the Union.
Later view: historians argue that the Famine made Ireland a more commercial but more unequal and emigrant society, with a prosperous farmer class above a shrinking labouring poor.
notes.tip: For 'how far' questions, give a paired judgement: a benefit and a limit for each theme, then weigh them.

keyTerms.definition: Money or land given by a bride's family on marriage, which after the Famine decided who could marry and who could inherit a farm.
The system in which a small landlord class owned almost all the land and let it to tenants, who had no security of tenure and could be evicted.
A tenant with a large holding who gained in wealth and influence after the Famine as small holdings were consolidated.
The joining of small plots into larger farms after the Famine, which ended the cottier class.
Emigration in which settled relatives and neighbours sent passage money and information to draw others abroad.
The state-funded primary school system set up in 1831 to give combined literary education to children of all denominations.
Non-denominational university colleges at Belfast, Cork and Galway, founded in 1845 and opened in 1849, which the Catholic Church condemned.
The Catholic institution founded in Dublin in 1854 under John Henry Newman as an alternative to the Queen's Colleges.
The 1849 Act that allowed heavily indebted estates to be sold, bringing new owners to many Irish estates.
The cloth made from flax whose mechanised production was the basis of Belfast's industrial growth.
